reception.text: The Associated Press moved the proclamation the day it was signed, and the Marshalltown, Iowa Evening Times-Republican printed the full text on its front page that afternoon.

Over the next few days papers from California to South Dakota, Ohio, Indiana, New Mexico and Iowa carried it, often on page one and often in full; its closing line appears on 106 digitized pages in Chronicling America alone.
reception.source: Chronicling America and California Digital Newspaper Collection sweep

reception.text: Headline writers singled out the passage mourning McKinley, with heads such as "Refers to Nation's Sad Loss."
reception.source: San Francisco Call, November 3, 1901; Morning Press (Santa Barbara), November 3, 1901

reception.text: The San Jose Mercury-News praised it as "characteristic of the man," saying he "says something" rather than stringing together platitudes.
The text was cabled to Manila and drew a second round of coverage there in mid-November.
The San Francisco Call's editorial page returned to the "duty to his fellow men" line, and the Healdsburg Tribune built a full essay on the history of Thanksgiving proclamations around Roosevelt's.
reception.source: San Francisco Call, November 13, 1901; Healdsburg Tribune, November 28, 1901

reception.text: The only jokes found aimed elsewhere, at the coming election and at the cost of cabling the proclamation to the Philippines; no contemporary objection to the proclamation has been found.
reception.source: Los Angeles Herald, November 6, 1901; Marysville Daily Appeal, November 17, 1901

legacy.text: The yearly presidential Thanksgiving proclamation, unbroken since Lincoln's of 1863, has continued to the present; Roosevelt signed one every year of his presidency.
The date rested on custom until Franklin Roosevelt moved Thanksgiving a week early in 1939, 1940 and 1941, splitting the states over which Thursday to keep.

related.note: Roosevelt's first proclamation, mourning McKinley; printed directly before this one as [No. 11.].

later_actions.text: Franklin Roosevelt's Proclamation 2373 set Thanksgiving a week before the last Thursday of November, on November 23.
A joint resolution fixed Thanksgiving by law as the fourth Thursday of November, beginning after 1941.

uncertain: Whether the large Eastern dailies, thinly represented in the digitized collections searched, carried any criticism of the proclamation.

legacy.text: Congress settled the date after House Joint Resolution 41 passed naming the last Thursday; the Senate changed it to the fourth Thursday, the House agreed on December 19, 1941, and Thanksgiving 1942 was the first held under statute.
legacy.source: Congressional Record, vol. 87, pt. 9, p. 10070; 55 Stat. 862
